source.title: Maintain an order summary read model

summary: Adds a CQRS projection that keeps per-customer order totals, and a migration that drops the legacy total column. The migration destroys data on deploy, and the projection adds to its totals again every time an event is replayed.

findings.summary: Column is dropped outright, and its data is gone on deploy
findings.rationale: The migration drops the legacy total column the moment it runs, with no copy taken anywhere first. Whatever those values held is deleted from production the instant the deploy reaches the database, and no part of this change reads them into the new columns beforehand. If anything downstream still reports on that total, or if the figures are ever needed to explain a historical number, the only remaining source is a database backup and a restore.
findings.suggestion: Split it into two deploys: this one stops writing and reading the column, and a later migration drops it once the data is confirmed unnecessary or has been copied into its replacement. If the column really is dead, say so in the migration and take an explicit backup of it first. The cost of waiting a release is one extra migration; the cost of being wrong is a restore.

findings.summary: Projection adds to the totals again whenever an event is replayed
findings.rationale: The handler increments the order count and adds to revenue on every delivery, and records nothing about which events it has already applied. Event handlers see the same event more than once as a matter of course, through broker retries and through the replay that rebuilds a read model, so the totals climb above the truth each time it happens. Nothing in the row says which events produced it, so a wrong total cannot be explained or repaired except by rebuilding from scratch, which relies on the same unsafe handler.
findings.suggestion: Record each applied event id against the summary row and skip an event already recorded, in the same transaction as the update, so a replay is a no-op rather than a second increment. Where the projection is derived rather than accumulated, recomputing the totals from the orders table is stronger still, because it makes the handler naturally repeatable.

findings.summary: The rollback restores the column but not what was in it
findings.rationale: The down migration adds the column back, so a rollback leaves the schema right and the data missing: every row comes back holding null. That is worth knowing before somebody rolls back expecting the old reports to work again, because the schema check will pass and the numbers will be empty.
findings.suggestion: Say in a comment that the rollback is structural only, or take the backup the previous point asks for so a restore has something to restore from. A down that cannot really undo the up is better documented than trusted.
